notes: STAND-IN (read as its own source, not used to confirm the article): Dreyer, J. 2013. The effects of lake-derived midges on terrestrial ecosystems and arthropod communities. PhD dissertation (Zoology), University of Wisconsin–Madison; https://asset.library.wisc.edu/1711.dl/UZG4CXUJJTCRR8U/R/file-25983.pdf (saved as docs/research_notes/fetched/v2/Dreyer_etal_2015.thesis2013.pdf). Chapter 1, 'Transfer of biomass and nutrients to a lake shoreline via aquatic insects' (printed p. 1, PDF p. 14), is the Mývatn emergence–deposition study of 2008–2011. What it says on the paper's points: (1) N and P: 'Since midges are approximately 10% N and 1% P by mass (Fagan et al. 2002, Gratton et al. 2008)' (printed p. 14, PDF p. 27) — literature values, by mass (dry mass implied by the deposition units), not measured at Mývatn. (2) No Mývatn figure for insects 'never returning': the introduction says 'as much as 97% of aquatic insects (~10% N by mass) remaining on land (Jackson and Fisher 1986)' (printed p. 2, PDF p. 15) and '75-99% of stream secondary productivity may be exported to land as insect biomass' (Jackson and Fisher 1986, Gray 1989, Petersen et al. 1999; printed p. 3, PDF p. 16) — stream studies. If the article's text is the same, §3.2.5's '70–99 % … (Dreyer et al. 2015)' misattributes stream literature to a Mývatn result. (3) Distance: 'Midge abundance on land peaked 20-25 meters from the lake with 70% occurring in the first 100 meters' (abstract, printed p. 1) — abundance in aerial traps; the deposition model puts ~35 % within 50 m and '>60% of midge deposition' within 100 m (printed p. 14, PDF p. 27). Traps overestimated deposition 20–30-fold. Other values: emergence 75 t dry mass yr⁻¹ (3 g dw m⁻² yr⁻¹) in 2008 down to 3.3 t in 2011; deposition within 50 m slightly above 100 kg dw ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in 2008 and ~50, 30 and 4 in 2009–2011, i.e. 0.4–10 kg N and 0.04–1 kg P ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (lake area 3,800 ha). The published article must be read before any of the four claims is confirmed; the human's library copy is the route.
